name: Civet

card.summary: A musky animal-derived fragrance material, historically taken from civets, used in perfumery to give scent depth and longevity.
card.note: Animal welfare concerns; most perfumery now uses synthetic substitutes.

quick.overview:
Civet is a strongly musky secretion from civets, prized in perfumery as a scent and as a stabiliser that helps fragrances last. Wearing fragrance is a grooming step people use to make a good impression.

The secretion comes from glands near the animal's genitals and has historically been collected from African civets. Today synthetic substitutes are available, and animal welfare groups object to harvesting.
quick.how: Most people meet civet only as a note in a finished perfume or cologne, not as a raw material. It is a fragrance ingredient, applied as part of a scent rather than used directly.
quick.risks: Welfare groups such as World Animal Protection say harvesting is cruel. Fragrance ingredients can cause skin reactions in some people.

lead: Civet musk is a secretion produced by civets that has long been used in perfumery, both as a fragrance in its own right and as a stabiliser that helps a perfume hold.[1] The African civet has historically been the main source.[1]
People use it, usually through finished perfumes, as part of grooming and personal scent. Shakespeare's As You Like It mentions the civet cat as a source of courtiers' perfumes.[1]

Musk can be taken by killing the animal and removing glands or by scraping secretions from a living animal, with live scraping preferred today; civets are kept in captivity in Ethiopia for this purpose.[1] Animal welfare organisations object to the practice, and synthetic substitutes are available.[1]

chain: Civet musk added to a fragrance
Pleasant lasting scent on the wearer
angle.text: Perfumers use civet as a stabiliser and musky note so a fragrance lasts longer on the wearer.[1]

paras: Both male and female civets produce the strong-smelling secretion.[1] It is described as musky and is prized in perfumery.[1]

The African civet has historically been the main source, and the animal appears in English literature as a source of perfume.[1] Collection by scraping from living animals is the preferred method today, and captive civet keeping occurs in Ethiopia.[1]

Animal rights groups including World Animal Protection object that harvesting civet musk is cruel.[1] Synthetic substitutes exist and, together with ethical concerns, have led to the practice of raising civets for musk declining.[1]

Palm civets sold in live animal markets in Guangdong were found to carry SARS-related coronaviruses, and genomic studies support bat-to-civet-to-human transmission in the 2002-2003 SARS epidemic.[2] This concerns live animal trade rather than perfume use.
